query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled amount (~3 at%) of tungsten during alloy synthesis will improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy by refining its microstructure and hindering dislocation motion.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy composed of five or more principal elements (each in the range of 5–35 at%) without any deliberate tungsten addition.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 3 at% tungsten into the alloy composition during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Test the alloy under elevated temperatures (approximately 800°C to 1000°C) under mechanical loads typical of extreme operating environments.
generation.structural_mediator: W tungsten is expected to promote grain boundary stabilization and form finely dispersed tungsten-rich precipitates, leading to a refined grain microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The formation of tungsten-rich precipitates and grain refinement are anticipated to impede dislocation motion and enhance resistance to creep, thereby improving the alloy's yield strength and high-temperature stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-added alloy is predicted to exhibit improved high-temperature mechanical properties (e.g., increased yield strength and reduced creep rates) relative to the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: The original titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without tungsten, processed under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to alloys within the compositional window defined by at least five principal elements (each 5–35 at%) and operating in the temperature range of roughly 800°C to 1000°C. Adding tungsten well beyond ~3 at% may induce phase instabilities or deleterious microstructural changes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement is uncertain and subject to experimental verification, though a meaningful improvement is anticipated if the mechanism holds.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one as the baseline titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy and one with the addition of approximately 3 at% tungsten. Process both samples identically. Conduct mechanical testing (yield strength and creep tests) under elevated-temperature conditions (800°C to 1000°C). Complement these tests with microstructural characterization (grain size analysis using SEM/TEM or XRD, and assessment of precipitate formation).
measurements: Creep rate or time-to-failure under constant load
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-added alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance (or if microstructural analysis fails to show evidence of grain refinement and tungsten-rich precipitates) compared to the baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a small, controlled amount of a refractory element (e.g., tungsten) to a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to an otherwise identical material lacking tungsten.
drafts.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy containing five or more principal elements (present in 5–35 at% each) with no deliberate refractory element additions.
drafts.intervention: Introduce approximately 3 at% tungsten into the alloy composition during alloy synthesis.
drafts.conditions: Test the alloy under elevated-temperature conditions (e.g., 800°C to 1000°C) under mechanical loads typical of extreme operating environments.
drafts.structural_mediator: W addition is expected to refine the microstructure by promoting grain boundary stabilization and forming finely dispersed tungsten-rich precipitates.
drafts.mechanism: The tungsten precipitates and refined grain structure are anticipated to impede dislocation motion and enhance creep resistance, thereby increasing yield strength and overall high-temperature stability.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-containing alloy should exhibit increased high-temperature yield strength and reduced creep rates (approximately a 15–25% improvement) compared to the baseline titanium–nickel alloy.
drafts.baseline: The original titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without tungsten, prepared under identical processing conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable in the compositional window defined by five or more principal elements (each with 5–35 at%) and an operating temperature range of roughly 800°C to 1000°C. Exceeding the tungsten concentration (e.g., above 5 at%) may lead to phase instability or undesirable microstructural changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one with the baseline titanium–nickel high-entropy composition and one with the addition of approximately 3 at% tungsten. Process both samples under identical conditions. Subject the samples to mechanical testing (yield strength and creep tests) at elevated temperatures (in the 800°C to 1000°C range) and perform microstructural analysis (grain size and precipitate distribution assessment).
measurements: Precipitate composition and dispersion via SEM/TEM or XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-added alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (at least 15% increase in yield strength and meaningful creep resistance improvement) over the baseline or if microstructural modifications (such as grain refinement or formation of tungsten-rich precipitates) are absent, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
